title: Binary search
summary: Find anything in a sorted list of a million items in about 20 steps.

cards.title: The guessing game
cards.body:
I'm thinking of a number from 1 to 100. You guess 50. I say "higher". You just threw away **half** the numbers in one question.

Keep halving: 100 → 50 → 25 → 13 → 7 → 4 → 2 → 1. At most **7 guesses**. That's binary search.
`lo` and `hi` mark the part that could still contain the answer. Dim boxes have been ruled out.

cards.title: The code
cards.body: Why `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2`? If `lo` and `hi` are both huge, `lo + hi` can **overflow** an int. This exact bug sat in Java's standard library binary search for years until it was found in 2006.

cards.title: O(log n)
cards.body:
Each step halves the range. Starting from n items you reach 1 after **log₂ n** steps.

- 1,000 items → ~10 steps
- 1,000,000 items → ~20 steps
- 1,000,000,000 items → ~30 steps

The one requirement: the data must be **sorted**. Binary search on unsorted data gives wrong answers, silently.

cards.title: Slot machines use this
cards.body:
A slot reel has symbols with different **weights** (say 7s are rare, cherries are common). To turn a random number into a symbol, games store running totals of the weights and binary-search the random number in them.

You'll build exactly that in the **Slot Math Lab**.

cards.question: A sorted list has 4,096 items. What is the maximum number of steps binary search needs?
cards.explain: 2¹² = 4,096, so about 12 halvings, plus one final check. Compare that with up to 4,096 for linear search.

cards.question: You run binary search for 6 on `[9, 2, 6, 1]` (unsorted). What happens?
choices: It may say 6 is missing even though it's there
cards.explain: Binary search assumes order when it throws half away. On unsorted data it can throw away the half that contained the answer. (The app's visualizer sorts first to protect you; real code won't.)

cards.title: Build it: lowerBound
cards.body: Implement `lowerBound`: the first index whose value is `>=` x. It's the most useful version of binary search (it's what `std::lower_bound` does) and the hardest to get exactly right. Write the invariant first.
